columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: Sold to Yahoo! in 2013 for USD 1.1B; Yahoo later wrote down much of that value.
Acquired by Automattic (WordPress.com’s parent) in August 2019 for <USD 3M, about 0.3% of Yahoo’s purchase price, and run as an Automattic subsidiary complementary to WordPress.com.
As of 2025, still active with an estimated ~135M monthly active users and 600M+ blogs; historically influential in fandom, social justice, and creative communities at its mid-2010s peak.

strengths.title: Rich expressive, creative culture
strengths.detail: Historically a hub for fandoms, memes, art, social commentary, and queer/alternative communities; still a vibrant space for niche cultural exchange.

strengths.title: Flexible multimedia microblogging
strengths.detail: Posts can combine text, images, GIFs, audio, and video; reblogging encourages remixing and layered commentary.

strengths.title: Strong tagging and discovery for niche topics
strengths.detail: Tagging and reblog networks surface niche content and foster communities around aesthetics, fandoms, and ideas.

strengths.title: Complementary to WordPress ecosystem
strengths.detail: Automattic’s stewardship and planned ActivityPub integration may deepen interoperability with WordPress and the broader Fediverse.

weaknesses.title: Massive value collapse and strategic drift
weaknesses.detail: From a USD 1.1B acquisition to a <USD 3M sale, a cautionary tale about monetizing cultural communities under corporate pressure.

weaknesses.title: Policy and content moderation shocks
weaknesses.detail: Changes (e.g. adult content bans under Verizon/Yahoo) alienated core users and contributed to decline in usage and cultural relevance.

weaknesses.title: Profitability challenges and perceived decline
weaknesses.detail: Frequently reported as loss-making; layoffs and restructuring within Automattic underscore ongoing business struggles.

weaknesses.title: Less mainstream relevance vs newer platforms
weaknesses.detail: Now overshadowed by Instagram, TikTok, and X, best understood as a niche, culture-heavy microblogging platform, not a primary mass-market social app.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. Tumblr is microblogging and social media platform for multimedia posts, reblogs, and creative / fandom communities. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

Tumblr is a microblogging and social media platform where people share multimedia posts to short-form blogs, follow others, and participate in creative, fandom, and cultural communities. Official site.

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and Tumblr side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On Tumblr you can use Newsletters and Community & Messaging as first-class product jobs. The job is hanging out, announcements, and live conversation, not packaging knowledge into something strangers can browse later.

Using Kahana with Tumblr

You can use both. Tumblr keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep live conversation on Tumblr. Pin a Kahana hub or Club link in a channel, discuss live there, and assign the next ebook, video, or course from Kahana so the syllabus is not buried in the thread.
